Tuition, Paychecks, and Student Loans: Is a Four-Year Degree Worth it?

by Colton Murphy, Group 32

Picking a college is one of the biggest money investments people make, and the price tags are all over the place. Some cost under $15,000 a year once you add up tuition, housing, books and everything else. On the other hand some cost close to $100,000. So it’s fair to ask if the investment is worth it? I dug into data from the U.S. Department of Education’s College Scorecard, which tracks cost and student outcomes for nearly every college in the country to find out. I focused on 1,682 schools that mainly give out bachelor’s degrees and that report both their cost and how much their students go on to earn.

The Big Picture: Does a Degree Really Pay Off at All?

Source: U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics Earnings and unemployment rates by educational attainment, 2025[Chart]. Retrieved November 23, 2026 from [https://www.bls.gov/emp/graphics/unemployment-rates-and-earnings.htm]

Before comparing colleges to each other it helps to know whether a bachelor’s degree is worth it in general. This chart from the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics says yes on average. In 2025, a typical full time worker with a bachelor’s earned $1,578 a week compared to $966 for someone with a high school diploma. That’s about 60% more or roughly $31,800 more per year which is a massive gap. Degree holders were also less likely to be out of work with a 2.8% unemployment compared to 4.3% for high school graduates. So a degree pays off on average. The real question is how much you should pay for one.

Explore It Yourself: Cost vs. Earnings

This chart compares the cost of attendance vs the median earnings of a student 10 years after starting college . Each dot is a different college. Dots farther right cost more per year, and dots higher up are colleges whose students earn more at the median. The colors show what kind of school it is, blue for public, orange for private nonprofit and green for private for profit.

How to use it: Hover over any dot to see the school’s name, location, cost, earnings, graduation rate and typical student loan debt. Click and drag a box over a group of dots and the bottom chart updates to show how earnings grow for the schools you picked 6, 8, and 10 years after starting college. You can double click to clear your box. You can also use the pick a state dropdown to highlight one state’s schools. The bottom chart then only shows that state.

What I see is that there’s a lot of spread at every price. More expensive schools do tend to have higher earnings, especially the very expensive ones in the top right. But plenty of $20,000-per-year public schools match or beat private schools that cost two to three times as much.

Same Earnings, Half the Price

This chart boils the scatter plot down to one comparison. For each type of school, the light gray bar is the typical yearly cost and the purple bar is the typical earnings 10 years after starting college. Public schools cost about $25,600 a year and the private non-profits cost about $52,200, roughly twice as much, but their former students end up earning almost exactly the same, around $59,000. Private for-profit schools land in the middle on price but at the bottom on earnings. I made this chart myself in Python using College Scorecard data. The code is in my (analysis noteboook)

The Cost After Graduation: Student Loans

The price of college doesn’t end at graduation. Most students borrow, and the loan payments follow them for years. The top chart shows each school’s typical (median) student loan debt at graduation against its typical earnings 10 years after starting. Drag a box over any group of dots, and the bottom chart shows what share of a typical monthly paycheck goes to the monthly loan payment (Debt numbers are missing for 67 schools, so they don’t appear here.) I also made this chart myself in Python using College Scorecard data. The code is in my (analysis noteboook)

Two things stand out. First, borrowing more doesn’t mean earning more. The dots don’t trend upward from left to right, so schools where students take on bigger loans don’t seem to produce higher earners. Second, for-profit students get hit twice. Their typical debt is the highest and they also earn the least. Across all schools a typical for-profit graduate’s loan payment takes about 9% of their monthly paycheck, about double what public school graduates pay and well above the 5.3% that private non-profits pay.

What This Means

The takeaway is that a higher price tag doesn’t guarantee a bigger paycheck, and bigger loans don’t either. For a lot of students, a public school can deliver the same typical earnings for about half the cost, with smaller loan payments taking less of each paycheck after graduation. That said, earnings numbers only include students who got federal financial aid, like Pell grants or federal loans. They also include students who started at a school but didn’t finish which may pull down earnings. So, use this as a starting point when comparing school outcomes not the final word.
